item.text: {"question_id":"6B.9","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s administration advanced institution-building, but the evidence supports partial construction rather than demonstrated durable institutions beyond personal rule. The PDL-145T had a national, decentralized mandate, multiple implementing agencies, public and partner financing, and reported progress toward schools, health centres, and administrative buildings; however, financing was planned and completion and quality were not independently verified (BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0010-E004; BATCH-0019-E009). The administration also operated within a formal victim-reparation framework with statutory governance, dedicated services, a mediator, a board, a professional directorate, and specified funding sources, including budget subsidies and mining royalties, but no supplied evidence confirms 2023 staffing, disbursement, or reach (BATCH-0029-E001). A 2022 budget allocation for child protection and a transition toward program budgeting provide relevant pre-2023 institutional and funding context, but neither execution nor results are established, and the national child-protection policy and Children’s Council arrangements remained incomplete or pending in the reported period (BATCH-0012-R01-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E005). The 2022 governance-budget decree supplied statutory controls, audit structures, treasury planning, and publication requirements, yet the evidence does not show compliance, operational independence, or corrective action in practice (BATCH-0029-E005). The health-coverage financing mechanisms are reported retrospectively and do not establish 2023 collection, expenditure, or coverage (BATCH-0020-E006). Social-protection arrangements show ministry policy responsibility and technical-agency delivery, but remained substantially donor-funded and aimed toward a future government-funded national system; dissolution of the Social Fund paused disbursements during transition (BATCH-0026-E005; BATCH-0017-E002). Professional and operational resilience was also constrained by insecurity, insufficient judges and resources, corruption, political and military interference, and a dysfunctional justice system, although UNDP-supported recruitment and training and selected 2023 justice outputs provide some countervailing evidence (BATCH-0011-E005; BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0009-E004). Overall, the period shows statutory designs, administrative mechanisms, and some implementation, but not reliable funding, fully demonstrated professional operation, transparent compliance, or resilience beyond personal
